 Kailey Hagen, CFP®, The Motley Fool Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:20 PM EDT 4 min read Most retirees lean on Social Security for much of their income. Yet the average check was built to replace only part of a paycheck. 
 As of September 2026, the average retired-worker benefit is $2,088.79 per month, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). That adds up to $25,065.48 per year.

 What typical senior households spend 
 A household headed by someone 65 or older spends $61,432 per year, based on the 2024 BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey, the most recent data available. This budget represents the reality for millions of households. The average benefit represents only a portion of that necessary cash flow. 
 Housing and healthcare often dominate the conversation for those on a fixed income. However, transportation and food are also significant line items that can stretch a monthly check. Here's a look at the breakdown in average annual spending by category as of 2024. 
 Category 
 Annual spending 
 Housing 
 $22,193 
 Healthcare 
 $7,799 
 Transportation 
 $9,538 
 Food 
 $7,940 
 All other 
 $13,962 
 Total 
 $61,432 
 Housing represents the single largest obligation for most seniors. Even those who have paid off their mortgages still face property taxes, insurance, and maintenance. These essential costs don't wait for a check to arrive. 
 Closing the gap between checks and costs 
 The average annual benefit of $25,065.48 covers only 41% of that annual senior-household spending. This gap exists by design. Social Security was built to replace 40% of pre-retirement income, not the whole thing. 
 This leaves an annual shortfall of $36,366.52. You'd have to cover this money some other way, whether from savings, a pension, or part-time work. For retirees who don't have a pension or deep savings, part-time work may be the only realistic choice. 
 The SSA calculates your benefit based on an average of your 35 highest-earning years. It adjusts earlier wages for inflation and runs them through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. This determines the baseline check you receive. 
 A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. This adjustment will add about $75 per month to the average benefit, since the current figures don't yet include it. These increases are designed to help buying power keep pace with inflation. 
 Story Continues A COLA helps prevent the gap from widening, but it doesn't close it. High inflation years can still erode the value of a check before the next adjustment arrives. Retirees must often adjust their budgets to stay ahead of rising costs. 
 The average check is a foundation, not a full budget, and the question is how to cover the rest. 
 For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide. 
 How to make your retirement budget more manageable 
 If you're trying to keep your retirement costs down to help your Social Security checks go further, housing and healthcare are the key items to focus on. Paying off your mortgage before retirement can help you stretch your savings much further because your biggest monthly payment will disappear. 
 If that's not an option, you might consider downsizing. But don't just assume that a smaller home will automatically be more affordable. It depends a lot on where you live. If housing costs have risen significantly in the area since you last purchased a home, even a smaller house may not save you as much as you expect. 
 For healthcare, prioritize a healthy diet, exercise, and good sleep. Take advantage of preventive services and free healthcare screenings through Medicare to catch potential problems early. 
 You may also want to invest in supplemental health insurance policies to help you cover what Social Security doesn't. These policies come with costs of their own, but they're usually easier to budget for than unpredictable hospital bills. 
 The $23,760 Social Security bonus most retirees completely overlook 
 If you're like most Americans, you're a few years (or more) behind on your retirement savings. But a handful of little-known "Social Security secrets" could help ensure a boost in your retirement income. For example: one easy trick could pay you as much as $23,760 more ... each year! Once you learn how to maximize your Social Security benefits, we think you could retire confidently with the peace of mind we're all after.
